About: Terminal Velocity — Raindrop in Air

Source

Concept
A raindrop falls through still air. Weight and air drag both act on it — watch the arrows and the speed.
Model
Quadratic drag: F_drag = −c·|v|·v, giving v(t) = v_T·tanh(g·t/v_T) from rest.
Serves
Newton's 2nd law with variable force; asymptotic approach to equilibrium; distinguishing steady-state from constant motion.

Guided Inquiry

1 · The setup

A raindrop is released from rest in still air. The pink arrow is its weight, always down. The blue arrow will be air drag, always up. At rest, drag is zero — find both arrows, then continue.

2 · Predict

What happens to the drop's speed as it falls further and further?

3 · Watch it happen

Press ▶ Play. Look at the right panel now. The green curve is v(t): it climbs, then flattens against the dashed line at v_T. The amber curve is a(t): it starts at g and decays toward zero.

The moment the two arrows on the drop become equal in length, a(t) has just touched zero and v(t) has flattened. That is terminal velocity.

4 · Predict: heavier drop

If you quadruple the drop's mass (keeping air the same), what happens to the terminal velocity?

5 · Explore

Now the whole simulation is yours. Try:

· Drag mass up — v_T rises as √m, and the drop takes longer to "settle".
· Drag drag coefficient up — v_T falls, and terminal is reached sooner.
· Watch that the spacing between drop positions on the left stops growing once v flattens on the right.

The key idea: terminal velocity is not the drop's maximum possible speed — it is the speed at which forces balance.

Terminal Velocity

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A drop is released from rest in still air. Its weight pulls it down and the air pushes back up on it, and the sim plots its speed and its acceleration against time.

What you'll learn

  • How the weight of the drop and the air drag on it combine to set its acceleration.
  • How the speed of the drop changes with time after release.
  • How the drop's motion depends on its mass and on the drag coefficient.
The drop is released from rest at the top. Air acts on it all the way down.

What's on screen

  • Drop and fall column (left): the drop falls down a column with a line every 5 m, and leaves a faint trail.
  • Weight arrow (pink): W, always pointing down.
  • Drag arrow (blue): Fd, the push of the air, always pointing up. Both arrows share one scale.
  • Green curve (right plot): speed v against time, on the left axis in m/s.
  • Amber curve: acceleration a against time, on the right axis in m/s².
See itOpen the sim with its opening values: m = 1.00 kg and c = 0.25 kg/m. Watch for: the drop at the top with the pink arrow W = 9.81 N, the blue arrow Fd = 0.00 N, and the speed at 0.00 m/s with the acceleration at 9.81 m/s².

Fixed: g = 9.81 m/s² and the drag force is c v². Moving either slider restarts the drop. The masses are far heavier than a real raindrop, but the physics is the same.

03

Drag grows with speed until it balances the weight

Two forces act on the drop: its weight W = mg down, and the drag Fd = c v² up. Newton's second law gives its motion:

m dv/dt = mg − c v²
v is the downward speed. The drag is quadratic in v.

At release v = 0, so there is no drag and a = g = 9.81 m/s². As v grows, c v² grows and the net force shrinks, so a falls. The speed keeps rising, but more slowly. When c v² = mg the net force is zero, a = 0 and v stops changing. For m = 1.00 kg and c = 0.25 kg/m this happens at 6.26 m/s, where Fd = 0.25 × 6.26² = 9.81 N = W.

See itPress Play with m = 1.00 and c = 0.25. Watch for: the green curve flattening near 6.26 m/s while the amber curve falls to 0, and the two arrows both at 9.81 N.
04

Terminal velocity is the speed where the forces balance

The constant speed at which a = 0 is the terminal velocity vT. Setting c vT² = mg gives:

vT = √(mg / c)
The sim shows it as the dashed line and as the Terminal vT readout.

Terminal velocity is a balance of forces, not a limit built into the sim. Both forces still act on the drop at vT. They cancel, so it moves at constant velocity. A drop released from rest approaches vT from below and does not pass it.

For m = 1.00 kg and c = 1.00 kg/m, vT = √(9.81 / 1.00) = 3.13 m/s.

See itSet m = 1.00 and c = 1.00, then press Play. Watch for: the dashed line labelled vT = 3.13 m/s and the green curve settling onto it, with the label ★ v = vT on the drop.
05

Quadrupling the mass only doubles the terminal velocity

Because vT = √(mg / c), it grows as √m and falls as 1/√c. A heavier drop needs more drag to balance its weight, and drag grows only as v², so vT rises more slowly than m.

m (kg)c (kg/m)vT (m/s)
0.250.253.13
1.000.256.26
4.000.2512.53
1.000.0514.01
1.001.003.13

Only the ratio m / c matters. Four times the mass and four times the drag coefficient give the same vT as m = 1.00 and c = 0.25.

See itSet m = 4.00 with c = 0.25, then press Play. Watch for: the dashed line at vT = 12.53 m/s, twice the 6.26 m/s at m = 1.00, and the weight arrow at 39.24 N.
06

The speed approaches terminal velocity gradually

Solving the equation of motion for a drop released from rest gives:

v(t) = vT tanh(gt / vT)    a(t) = g sech²(gt / vT)
The time scale is τ = vT / g.

After one τ the speed is 76% of vT, after 2τ it is 96%, and after 3τ it is 99.5%. It never reaches vT exactly. For m = 1.00 and c = 0.25, τ = 6.26 / 9.81 = 0.64 s. A larger vT means a larger τ, so a heavier drop takes longer to settle: τ = 1.28 s at m = 4.00.

See itSet m = 1.00 and c = 0.05, then press Play. Watch for: vT = 14.01 m/s and a green curve that needs about 3.8 s to reach 99% of that, against 1.7 s at c = 0.25.
07

Where it matters

  • Raindrops. A drop that fell 1 km with no air would reach about 140 m/s. Real drops settle at a few m/s up to about 9 m/s, depending on their size.
  • Parachutes. The drag coefficient is c = ½ρairCDA, so a bigger area A raises c and lowers vT. An open parachute cuts a skydiver's vT from roughly 55 m/s to about 5 m/s.
  • Vehicles. At top speed the air drag and other resistance together balance the engine's push, the same balance of forces as here.
Go deeper: when drag is not quadratic

The sim uses Fd = c v². This fits fast motion of objects that are not tiny. For very small, slow drops such as mist, the drag is proportional to v instead (Stokes drag, 6πηrv in a fluid of viscosity η), and vT then depends on the drop's radius in a different way. The sim does not model that case.

08

Summary

In one line. This sim lets you release a drop in air and change its mass and the drag coefficient, to see how weight and air drag together set its speed over time.

Key points

  • m dv/dt = mg − c v², so a = g at release and a falls to 0 when c v² = mg.
  • That balance gives vT = √(mg / c), which grows as √m and falls as 1/√c.
  • The speed follows v = vT tanh(gt / vT) and approaches vT over a time of a few τ = vT / g.

Common mix-ups

  • "At terminal velocity the forces have stopped acting." Both still act. They are equal and opposite, so the net force is zero.
  • "Four times the mass gives four times the terminal velocity." It gives two times, because vT grows as √m.
  • "The drop reaches vT at a fixed moment." It only approaches vT, and a heavier drop takes longer.

Things to try on your own

  • Predict the mass that gives vT = 10 m/s at c = 0.25, then set it and read the Terminal vT readout.
  • Set m = 4.00 and c = 1.00, and compare vT with the opening values.
  • Run the opening values and note the time at which the acceleration first reads 0.00 m/s².
